syllabusTopics: Ecosystem ecology: Concept of ecology, biotic and abiotic factors, species interactions
Concept of ecosystem, structural and functional aspects of pond and forest ecosystem
Food chain, food web, trophic level, ecological pyramids, productivity
Biogeochemical cycles: carbon and nitrogen cycles; concept of succession
Ecological adaptation: Concept of adaptation, hydrophytes and xerophytes
Ecological imbalances: Greenhouse effects and climate change, depletion of ozone layer, acid rain and biological invasion

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Energy and matter flow through ecosystems in food chains (linear) and food webs (networks). Trophic levels (producers → primary consumers → secondary → tertiary) structure these. Ecological pyramids (number, biomass, energy) visualise trophic structure; the pyramid of energy is always upright because ~90% of energy is lost at each transfer (10% rule).…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
Food chain: Producer (TL1) → Primary consumer (TL2) → Secondary consumer (TL3) → Tertiary consumer (TL4)
10% rule: only ~10% of energy transfers between trophic levels
GPP = total photosynthesis; NPP = GPP − plant respiration (R)

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: A food chain is LINEAR; a food web is a NETWORK of chains (more realistic).  ·  Producers (plants, phytoplankton) are at trophic level 1; herbivores at level 2; carnivores at level 3+.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: NEB expects the three ecological pyramids and when each can be inverted.  ·  The 10% rule and the always-upright energy pyramid are very common exam points.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Grassland food chain: grass → rabbit → fox → eagle (4 trophic levels).  ·  Pond food web: algae → mosquito larva → frog → snake → eagle; also algae → zooplankton → small fish → big fish.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: The pyramid of ENERGY is always upright; the pyramids of numbers and biomass CAN be inverted.  ·  An inverted pyramid of numbers occurs when one large organism supports many small ones (e.g., a tree with many insects).

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: Draw a food chain  ·  Draw a food web

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Energy pyramid = always upright (E-up).  ·  Number and biomass pyramids = CAN be inverted.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: Differentiate a food chain from a food web.  ·  Explain the three types of ecological pyramids.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Explain the three ecological pyramids.  ·  Explain why the pyramid of energy is always upright.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Food chain vs food web  ·  Trophic levels  ·  Ecological pyramids (number, biomass, energy)  ·  10% rule

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Food chain = linear; food web = network of chains.  ·  Trophic levels: TL1 producers, TL2 herbivores, TL3 carnivores, TL4+ top carnivores.  ·  Three pyramids: number, biomass, energy.  ·  Pyramid of energy is ALWAYS upright; number and biomass can be inverted.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The 10% rule (Lindeman, 1942) explains why food chains are usually 4–5 trophic levels long.  ·  A pyramid of energy is ALWAYS upright because energy is lost at each transfer (heat, respiration).

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: Define trophic levels and give one example of each.  ·  Calculate NPP from GPP and respiration (given values).

rows.label: More hints
rows.text: Define GPP and NPP; calculate NPP.  ·  Draw a food chain and a food web with examples.

rows.label: Extra solved
rows.text: Inverted pyramid of numbers: one oak tree (TL1) → many aphids (TL2) → a few ladybirds (TL3).  ·  Inverted pyramid of biomass: phytoplankton (TL1) → zooplankton (TL2) → small fish (TL3) in the ocean.

rows.label: MCQ drill
rows.text: Which ecological pyramid is ALWAYS upright? → C  ·  Approximately what percentage of energy transfers between trophic levels? → B

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: Food chain: a linear sequence of organisms where each is eaten by the next; transfers energy and matter (sun → producer → primary consumer → secondary consumer → tertiary consumer).  ·  Food web: a network of interconnected food chains; more realistic than a single chain; shows multiple feeding relationships.  ·  Trophic levels: TL1 producers (autotrophs), TL2 primary consumers (herbivores), TL3 secondary consumers (carnivores), TL4+ tertiary consumers.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: GPP and NPP  ·  Inverted pyramids  ·  Productivity

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Pyramid of energy: always upright; each level < the one below  ·  10% rule: ~10% energy transfers between levels.  ·  Productivity: GPP (total), NPP (GPP − respiration).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: NPP is the energy available to herbivores.  ·  An inverted pyramid of biomass occurs in aquatic ecosystems where phytoplankton (producers) have low standing biomass but high turnover.  ·  The 10% rule: only ~10% of energy transfers from one trophic level to the next; ~90% is lost as heat.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Productivity: GPP = 1000 gC/m²/yr; plant respiration = 500 gC/m²/yr → NPP = 500 gC/m²/yr.  ·  NPP = GPP − respiration is a calculation question.  ·  Give a Nepali food chain (e.g., grass → deer → tiger) and a pond food web.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Memorise the three pyramids (number, biomass, energy).  ·  Learn when each can be inverted (number, biomass).  ·  Explain the 10% rule and its significance.
